source.description: Practice spelling the following six words in katakana. Unlike the hiragana writing system, long vowels in katakana words are transcribed with a bar or "dash." For example: リー (りい in hiragana), カー (かあ in hiragana).

config.info: Practice spelling the following six words in katakana. Unlike the hiragana writing system, long vowels in katakana words are transcribed with a bar or "dash." For example: リー (りい in hiragana), カー (かあ in hiragana).

delivery.beat: Tom reveals one source word card at a time and Jenny checks the long-vowel bar only after the learner writes the word.

steps.evidence: Match spoken loanwords to labels before writing the new a- and ka-row signs.

steps.form: ア イ ウ エ オ / カ キ ク ケ コ / ガ ギ グ ゲ ゴ
steps.meaning: Read and write the a- and ka-rows, including voiced marks.
steps.contrast: Dakuten changes ka to ga; it is not decoration and must stay with the sign.
steps.workedExample: アサ begins with ア; カメラ begins with カ.

steps.activity: Hear the word, find its label, then identify whether a dakuten is required.

progressiveHints: Add dakuten only where the sound is voiced.

feedback.error: If dakuten is omitted or added to the wrong sign, the sound changes.
feedback.retry: Read the label aloud, check each voiced sound, and write it again.

progressiveHints: Read the full word before translating.

feedback.error: If a label is translated without decoding its signs, the reading evidence is missing.

learningObjectives: Read the the a-row and ka-row, with the ga marks in katakana.
Hand-write each new katakana shape with a steady stroke order.
Tell apart look-alike katakana by the direction and position of their small strokes.
Read familiar loanwords by joining one sound at a time.
Hear a word and choose the matching katakana spelling.

explanation.recap: Katakana-1 gave you the five vowel shapes. Those same five vowels now carry k, then the small dakuten marks that voice k into g.
explanation.intro: Katakana writes the same Japanese sound system you already know. Today the work is visual: learn the shapes in the a-row and ka-row, with the ga marks, then let a familiar word give each shape a job. Read in short beats; one katakana normally carries one sound.

grammarPoints.pattern: カタカナ 一字 = 一つの 音
grammarPoints.meaning: one katakana sign usually holds one Japanese sound
grammarPoints.explanation: Katakana is not an English spelling system. Read each sign in order and give it one clean Japanese beat. Long words are not rushed: カ・メ・ラ is ka-me-ra. When a word has a long bar, stretch the vowel before it gently.
grammarPoints.watchFor: Do not guess from English spelling. Trust the katakana sounds on the page.
grammarPoints.commonError: Trying to give one sign two English sounds. Keep a single beat for each sign.

examples.note: Read the signs one by one.
The word is built from steady beats.

grammarPoints.nameJa: だくてん・半だくてん
grammarPoints.meaning: small marks can change a consonant sound
grammarPoints.explanation: Some katakana gain two small dakuten strokes, and the ハ row can gain a small handakuten circle. These marks are not decoration. They change the sound, so keep them small but visible.
grammarPoints.watchFor: The marks sit at the upper right of the character they change.
grammarPoints.commonError: Writing the mark in the middle of the character, where it becomes hard to read.

examples.note: Two small strokes voice the sound.

mission.title: The label finder
mission.prompt: Find four katakana labels around you: on food, a screen, a book, or an imagined shop shelf. Read them aloud and keep one that you want to remember.
successCriteria: You identify four katakana words or labels.
You read each one in separate Japanese sound beats.
You write one word with the small marks in the right place if it has them.
You say one meaning without relying on an English spelling guess.
